screens.title: Application Modernization with Serverless and Containers
screens.narratorSegment: Modernization is about transforming how applications are designed and run so they take full advantage of the cloud. In this lesson we compare two dominant paradigms: serverless computing, where you hand operational concerns to the provider and pay for actual execution, and containerization, where you package runtime and dependencies for portability and control. You will learn core AWS services and when each approach fits common patterns like APIs, background processing, and long-running workloads. We’ll walk through a serverless A P I pattern that combines A P I Gateway, Lambda, and DynamoDB and a container workflow using Docker, Amazon ECS with Fargate, or Amazon EKS for Kubernetes. You’ll also see CI/CD integration using AWS Developer Tools and practical tuning tips for cost, performance, and observability. By the end you’ll be able to propose a modernization approach for a product catalog, explain trade-offs between pay-per-use and packaged portability, and identify key operational practices like rightsizing, tracing, and the principle of least privilege. Think about one legacy workload you know — which model would reduce operational overhead fastest and why?

keyIdea.title: Why modernization matters
keyIdea.text: Modernization aligns architecture with cloud characteristics: elasticity, operational simplicity, and cost control. Choosing serverless or containers depends on workload patterns, runtime needs, and operational preferences.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.6 › Overview
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Application Modernization with Serverless and Containers

Learn how to choose and design serverless and containerized architectures on AWS, integrate CI/CD, and optimize for cost and performance.

In this lesson
Compare serverless and containers, design event-driven APIs, build container images, and set up CI/CD pipelines.
Why it matters
Modern architectures reduce toil, improve scalability, and enable faster delivery cycles for critical applications.
Real outcome
You will be able to recommend serverless or container approaches and outline the CI/CD and monitoring practices that ensure safe production deployment.
Concept map
Serverless
API Gateway, Lambda, DynamoDB, EventBridge
Containers
Docker, ECS, Fargate, EKS
CI/CD & Ops
CodeBuild, CodePipeline, ECR, observability
Explore key topics to start: serverless patterns, containers and orchestration, CI/CD and optimization.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to evaluate the benefits and trade-offs of serverless and container architectures, design event-driven APIs using Lambda and A P I Gateway, and implement containerized services on ECS, Fargate, or EKS. You will also integrate CI/CD pipelines that deploy serverless applications and container images, and apply cost and performance optimization techniques specific to each model. Each objective ties a capability to an observable outcome: design diagrams, deployment artifacts, and measurable optimizations. For example, you’ll practice creating a serverless A P I and a container image, then wire them into a pipeline that builds, tests, and deploys. You’ll learn when to prefer Lambda’s event-driven scaling over Fargate’s runtime control, and how provisioning choices affect latency and cost. These skills are practical; they let you reduce operational overhead or provide portability, depending on the business need. As you study, think about how you would validate each objective with a short test or hands-on task.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Applied Outcomes
screens.narratorSegment: These applied objectives translate into artifacts and measurable outcomes. You will produce an event-driven A P I design that includes A P I Gateway routes, Lambda handlers, and a DynamoDB access pattern; a container image and deployment manifest for ECS Fargate or EKS; and a CI/CD pipeline that builds and deploys either a SAM package or a container image pushed to ECR. Measurement criteria include deployment time, cold-start latency for Lambda, per-invocation cost estimate, and container startup latency. We’ll show you how to instrument these outcomes with CloudWatch metrics and distributed tracing so you can verify improvements. A common misconception is that modernization always reduces cost — instead, modernization shifts costs and trade-offs: serverless can reduce idle infrastructure spend but may increase per-invocation costs for very high sustained throughput. Keep that in mind as you compare approaches and validate with simple metrics after deployment.

screens.title: Serverless Computing and AWS Lambda
screens.narratorSegment: Serverless computing is a cloud execution model where the provider manages servers and capacity so developers can focus on code. AWS Lambda exemplifies this: you upload a function, configure triggers, and Lambda runs the code on demand while scaling automatically. Common serverless use cases include short-lived microservice endpoints, data transformation jobs triggered by storage events, mobile backends, and chatbots. A concrete example is an image thumbnailer: when an image is uploaded to object storage, an event triggers Lambda to resize and store thumbnails. That pattern removes the need to manage servers but brings specific constraints. Functions have maximum execution durations and require you to design for short-lived, stateless work. Cold starts occur when a function is invoked after a period of inactivity; provisioned concurrency can reduce cold-start latency for latency-sensitive endpoints. A common misconception is thinking Lambda is suitable for every workload: long-running processes, heavy G P U workloads, or apps needing custom kernel modules are better suited to containers or EC2. As you design serverless components, apply the principle of least privilege for IAM roles, decouple services with queues to handle bursts, and measure per-invocation cost against expected throughput. Which part of your application can be refactored into short, stateless functions first?

keyIdea.title: Serverless claim
keyIdea.text: Serverless removes server management for short, event-driven workloads but requires stateless design and attention to cold-starts and execution limits.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.6 › Serverless Computing
Definition

AWS Lambda

Run code without managing servers. Pay-per-use billing and automatic scaling for event-driven workloads.

Why use it
  • Fast iteration for small units of work.
  • Automatic scaling with traffic.
  • Lower operational overhead for many scenarios.
Key Takeaway

Serverless fits short, stateless tasks. Use queues and event buses to decouple and absorb bursts.

Example
// Image thumbnailer example // Trigger: ObjectStore upload event function handler(event) { // fetch object, resize, save thumbnail }
Design considerations
  • Limit execution time and keep functions stateless.
  • Mitigate cold-starts with provisioned concurrency when needed.
  • Use IAM roles scoped to required resources only.
Common mistake
Treating functions like long-running services.
Pro tip
Push heavy or stateful work to containers or managed compute if duration or drivers are needed.

screens.title: Serverless API Pattern: API Gateway → Lambda → DynamoDB
screens.narratorSegment: A common serverless pattern for APIs uses A P I Gateway to accept HTTP requests, Lambda for business logic, and DynamoDB for low-latency data storage. The request enters A P I Gateway which handles authentication, throttling, and caching, then forwards the event to a Lambda function. The function performs validation and reads or writes to DynamoDB. For asynchronous work, the function can publish events to SNS or EventBridge or push messages to SQS for buffered processing. This pattern provides clear integration points: A P I Gateway for ingress policy, Lambda for execution with scoped IAM permissions to access a specific DynamoDB table, and messaging services to decouple long-running or unreliable downstream tasks. A concrete scenario is a product catalog read: a GET request to /products/{id} triggers a Lambda that reads DynamoDB with a single-key query and returns results. Misconceptions include assuming synchronous invocation is always best; for durability and smoothing bursts, buffer writes with SQS or event buses. When designing this flow, consider cold-starts for user-facing routes, set appropriate retries, and apply caching where reads are common. How would you design retries and idempotency for write operations to prevent duplication?

keyIdea.title: Pattern summary
keyIdea.text: API Gateway routes requests, Lambda implements logic, and DynamoDB provides fast, scalable storage. Use queues and event buses to decouple and scale reliably.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.6 › Serverless API Pattern
Process

API Gateway → Lambda → DynamoDB

Step 1: API Gateway
Handles routing, auth, quotas, and optional caching before invoking Lambda.
Step 2: Lambda
Executes validation and business logic with scoped IAM role to access DynamoDB.
Step 3: DynamoDB
Low-latency NoSQL storage suitable for single-key and single-table designs.
Design tip: use SQS for buffered writes and EventBridge for integrating multiple consumers without coupling Lambda to downstream services.
Concrete example

Product read request

GET /products/{product_id} → API Gateway validates auth → Lambda queries DynamoDB by product_id and returns item
Key Takeaway
This pattern gives clear separation of concerns and easy scaling for reads and writes when designed with decoupling.
Common mistake
Directly chaining many synchronous services in a single function, which increases failure blast radius.

screens.title: SAM Template Example for a Serverless API
screens.narratorSegment: Infrastructure-as-code lets you describe serverless resources and deploy them reproducibly. The Serverless Application Model, or SAM, provides a concise way to declare Lambda functions, A P I events, and DynamoDB tables. The template example in this chapter shows two functions, GetProductFunction and CreateProductFunction, each wired to an A P I event and granted the appropriate DynamoDB policy. When you deploy with a SAM workflow, the template becomes the single source of truth for configuration like memory, timeout, and attached policies. A concrete walkthrough: the GetProductFunction includes an Api event with a GET path mapping, which tells A P I Gateway to route GET requests for that path to this function. The ProductsTable resource uses PAY_PER_REQUEST billing to match serverless cost behavior. A common misunderstanding is forgetting to scope IAM policies — grant only the minimal permissions each function needs. After deployment, test the A P I and inspect CloudWatch logs to verify handler logic and identify cold-start patterns. In practice, keep templates modular and parameterized to support multiple environments. SAM Template Example for a Serverless API means sam templates define functions, events, and resources as code so deployments are repeatable and auditable.. In practical terms, understanding resources, events, and permissions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.6 › SAM Template
Template snippet
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: '2010-09-09' Transform: AWS::Serverless-2016-10-31 Description: A simple serverless API for managing products Resources: GetProductFunction: Type: AWS::Serverless::Function Properties: Handler: app.get_product_handler Runtime: python3.9 CodeUri: s3://your-code-bucket/get-product-function.zip MemorySize: 128 Timeout: 30 Policies: - DynamoDBReadPolicy: TableName: !Ref ProductsTable Events: Api: Type: Api Properties: Path: /products/{product_id} Method: GET ProductsTable: Type: AWS::DynamoDB::Table Properties: AttributeDefinitions: - AttributeName: product_id AttributeType: S KeySchema: - AttributeName: product_id KeyType: HASH BillingMode: PAY_PER_REQUEST
Walkthrough
This snippet declares a function, its runtime, handler, memory and timeout, and an API event. The table resource is declared alongside functions so permissions can be attached in the template. PAY_PER_REQUEST fits serverless billing by avoiding capacity planning.
Best practice
Attach least-privilege policies and parameterize bucket names and stage values for reuse across environments.
Common mistake
Bundling secrets or hard-coded ARNs into templates instead of using parameter store or secrets manager.
After deployment, verify the API endpoints and use CloudWatch logs to confirm handler runs and performance characteristics.

screens.title: Containerization and Docker
screens.narratorSegment: Containerization packages an application and all its dependencies into a lightweight, portable unit that runs consistently across environments. Docker is the de facto tool for building container images. Containers solve the "it works on my machine" problem by including runtime, libraries, and configuration in a single image. A short Dockerfile for a Node. js app illustrates the pattern: start from a base image, set a working directory, copy package metadata, install dependencies, copy source, expose a port, and define the startup command. This produces an image you can run locally and then push to a registry such as ECR. An important distinction is that containers provide greater control over runtime and long-running processes compared with serverless functions. They are preferable when you need custom runtime dependencies, long execution times, or G P U support. A misconception is equating containers with zero ops; orchestration and node management remain concerns unless you use a managed mode like Fargate. When creating images, optimize the build for smaller image sizes and security scanning so deployments remain fast and safe. What dependency could you remove or slim to reduce your image size?

keyIdea.title: Containers in brief
keyIdea.text: Containers package runtime and dependencies for portability and control; use them for longer-lived or specialized workloads.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.6 › Containerization
Definition

Dockerfile example

# Example Dockerfile for a Node.js application FROM node:16-alpine WORKDIR /app COPY package*.json ./ RUN npm install COPY . . EXPOSE 3000 CMD ["npm", "start"]
This sequence installs dependencies separately to leverage build cache, then copies source and defines the default command. Smaller base images and multi-stage builds reduce final image size.
Practical notes
  • Use multi-stage builds to remove build-time dependencies from final images.
  • Scan images for vulnerabilities and minimize layers for faster pulls.
  • Push images to ECR and reference them in task definitions or manifests.
Key Takeaway

Containers give runtime control and portability. Optimize image size and scan for security before deployment.

screens.title: ECS, Fargate, and EKS — Choosing an orchestration model
screens.narratorSegment: AWS provides multiple container orchestration options: Amazon ECS for a native, simple orchestration experience; AWS Fargate to run containers without managing instances; and Amazon EKS for Kubernetes-managed workloads. ECS is straightforward and integrates well with other AWS primitives. Choose ECS when you want simple task definition and cluster management with AWS integration. Fargate removes instance management completely — it is useful when you want the container model but prefer serverless operations for container workloads. EKS is the managed Kubernetes control plane: use EKS when you require Kubernetes APIs, portability across clouds, or advanced scheduling and extensibility. An example decision: if your team relies on Kubernetes tooling and helm charts, EKS preserves that workflow; if your application needs serverless-style operations and you do not need Kubernetes features, choose Fargate. A common misconception is that Fargate and Lambda are interchangeable; they are not. Fargate runs containers and supports longer running processes and custom runtimes, while Lambda is designed for short-lived functions. Consider operational skill, portability needs, runtime requirements, and cost model when deciding which orchestration fits your modernization plan. ECS, Fargate, and EKS — Choosing an orchestration model means pick ecs for native simplicity, fargate for serverless containers, and eks when kubernetes features and portability are required.. In practical terms, managed orchestration options and when to pick each. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.6 › ECS vs Fargate vs EKS
Amazon ECS
Managed orchestration
Simple cluster management, deep AWS integration. Choose for straightforward task-based workloads and teams that prefer AWS-native APIs.
AWS Fargate
Serverless containers
No instance management. Ideal when you want container portability without maintaining nodes and when workloads have variable scale.
Amazon EKS
Managed Kubernetes
Choose when Kubernetes APIs, portability, and advanced scheduling are required. Requires Kubernetes operational know-how.
Trade-off example
Fargate reduces ops but may cost more for very large, predictable fleets. EKS provides portability but increases operational complexity.
Key Takeaway
Match orchestration to your team's skills, runtime needs, and portability requirements rather than adopting a tool by default.

screens.title: Building and Deploying a Container Image
screens.narratorSegment: Creating a containerized application follows a short cycle: author a Dockerfile, build an image, push it to a registry like ECR, and deploy via a task definition or Kubernetes manifest. The example Dockerfile in this chapter uses a Node. js base image, installs dependencies, and exposes a port. After building locally with the docker build command, tag the image for ECR and push it. In ECS, create a task definition that references the ECR image and then run the task as a service either on EC2-backed clusters or on Fargate for serverless operations. For Kubernetes, you apply a deployment manifest and expose it with a LoadBalancer service. A typical command sequence is: build, tag with the ECR repository URI, docker push, then update the service to use the new image. Common mistakes include not scanning images for vulnerabilities and embedding credentials in the image. Always use IAM roles for tasks and scan images before pushing. Consider using multi-stage builds to reduce image size and speed up pulls, which improves startup time in production. Building and Deploying a Container Image means build images with optimized dockerfiles, push to ecr, and deploy via ecs/fargate or eks with proper task roles and image scanning.. In practical terms, dockerfile, build, push to ecr, and run on ecs/fargate. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.6 › Build & Deploy
Commands (conceptual)
# Build locally docker build -t my-webapp:latest . # Tag for ECR docker tag my-webapp:latest 123456789012.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/my-webapp:latest # Push to ECR docker push 123456789012.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/my-webapp:latest # Update ECS service to use new image (conceptual) # ecs update-service --cluster my-cluster --service my-service --force-new-deployment
Deployment notes
Use task roles and secrets stored in parameter store or secrets manager rather than bake-time variables. For Fargate, you do not manage nodes, only task definitions and scaling policies.
Pro tip
Use multi-stage builds and remove dev dependencies to speed deploys and reduce attack surface.
Pitfall
Forgetting to grant the task role ECR pull permissions or to configure appropriate security groups for networking.
Ask: what parts of your CI pipeline should verify image security before deployment?

screens.title: CI/CD for Serverless and Containers
screens.narratorSegment: CI/CD pipelines automate the repetitive steps of building, testing, and deploying modern applications. AWS Developer Tools—CodeCommit, CodeBuild, CodeDeploy, and CodePipeline—integrate directly with serverless and container targets. For serverless apps, a typical pipeline builds code, packages a SAM artifact, runs unit and integration tests, and then executes a deployment step that updates the CloudFormation stack or SAM application. For containers, the pipeline builds a Docker image in CodeBuild, pushes it to ECR, and then updates an ECS task definition or triggers a Kubernetes rollout. Key CI/CD practices include immutable artifacts, automated tests, and deployment strategies such as blue/green or canary to reduce risk. A common misconception is that CI/CD only speeds delivery; it also enforces consistency and improves rollback safety. Ensure pipelines run image scans and integration tests before promoting artifacts to production. When integrating serverless deployments, consider how to manage permissions so the pipeline has least privilege and can perform only its required tasks. What tests would you add to validate a serverless function's behavior in a pipeline? Module 4 › Chapter 4.6 › CI/CD
Flow
  1. Source commit triggers pipeline (CodeCommit or other).
  2. Build stage builds artifact: SAM package or Docker image (CodeBuild).
  3. Test stage runs unit and integration tests and security scans.
  4. Deploy stage applies changes: CloudFormation/SAM deploy or ECS/EKS rollout.
Use immutable artifacts and promote them between stages rather than rebuilding in each environment.
Example checks
  • Unit tests for function logic and containerized app code.
  • Integration tests that hit a staging endpoint.
  • Image vulnerability scan and secret detection.
Operational tip
Use canary or blue/green deployments to reduce blast radius when updating production services.

screens.title: Cost and Performance Optimization
screens.narratorSegment: Optimizing for cost and performance requires understanding the billing and scaling models of serverless and container platforms. For Lambda, costs are driven by memory allocation and execution time. Rightsize memory to match C P U needs because increasing memory can also increase C P U and reduce execution time, which may lower cost for C P U-bound functions. Use provisioned concurrency for latency-sensitive endpoints to reduce cold-starts, but balance the fixed cost against expected traffic. For containers, choose between EC2 instances or Fargate; Fargate removes instance management but pricing differs, so use Fargate for variable workloads and EC2-backed clusters with autoscaling for consistently high throughput. Implement task and pod autoscaling based on appropriate metrics — C P U, memory, or custom application-level metrics. Spot instances can reduce cost for fault-tolerant workloads. Monitoring-driven scaling is essential: combine CloudWatch alarms with autoscaling policies, and verify behavior through load tests. A common mistake is turning on aggressive autoscaling without proper cooldowns, which causes thrashing. Always validate cost impact in a staging environment and set budgets and alerts to detect unexpected spend. Cost and Performance Optimization means right-size resources, use provisioned concurrency only when necessary, and apply autoscaling and spot instances thoughtfully to balance cost and performance.. In practical terms, rightsizing, concurrency, and auto-scaling strategies. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.6 › Cost & Performance
Serverless tips
  • Measure function execution time and tune memory to optimize cost.
  • Use provisioned concurrency for latency-sensitive endpoints only.
  • Buffer bursts with SQS to avoid synchronous scaling costs.
Container tips
  • For predictable load, right-size EC2 instances or use reserved capacity.
  • Use Fargate for variable workloads to avoid over-provisioning.
  • Consider Spot for fault-tolerant tasks to reduce compute costs.
Key Takeaway
Optimization is measurement-driven. Validate tuning with load tests and cost estimates before applying to production.

screens.title: Monitoring, Tracing, and Security
screens.narratorSegment: Observability and security are essential when modernizing applications. Implement monitoring with CloudWatch metrics for Lambda durations and errors, and use X-Ray for distributed tracing so you can see how requests flow across A P I Gateway, Lambda, and downstream services. For containerized apps, integrate Prometheus and Grafana or use CloudWatch Container Insights to gather C P U, memory, and network telemetry. Tracing helps pinpoint latency hotspots and the cause of errors across mixed architectures. Security starts with IAM: assign least-privilege roles to Lambda functions and task roles for containers so each workload can access only required resources. Scan container images for vulnerabilities before pushing to ECR and use private registries or repository policies to control access. A common mistake is under-instrumenting: without traces and logs, diagnosing production issues becomes slow and risky. Build automated alerts for error rates and increases in latency, and include observability checks in your deployment pipeline so new versions meet performance and security baselines before going to production. What trace would you examine first if users report intermittent timeouts? Monitoring, Tracing, and Security means combine logs, metrics, and traces for observability; enforce least-privilege iam and image scanning for secure operations.. In practical terms, observability and least-privilege for modernized applications. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Modernizing the E-commerce Product Catalog (Activity)
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity asks you to modernize a monolithic product catalog into two proposals: a serverless design and a containerized design. For the serverless proposal, identify core components: A P I endpoint with A P I Gateway, read and write logic in Lambda functions, DynamoDB for storage, and EventBridge or SQS for asynchronous updates. Describe how reads use a single-key DynamoDB query and how writes publish events for downstream processors. For the containerized proposal using Fargate, identify components: an ALB or A P I Gateway for routing, a Fargate service running containerized application code, and a managed relational or Aurora database if relational semantics are required. Think about migration effort: serverless may require redesigning state and data access patterns, while containers allow reusing existing application code with fewer logic changes. Discuss trade-offs: serverless yields operational simplicity and pay-per-use but imposes execution limits and stateless patterns; containers offer runtime control and support long-running or G P U workloads but require image management and orchestration considerations. Conclude by selecting which approach you would recommend for this product catalog and justify with traffic patterns, latency needs, and development team skills.

Serverless proposal
Components: API Gateway, Lambda for read/write, DynamoDB for storage, EventBridge or SQS for async updates and decoupling. Use PAY_PER_REQUEST billing for DynamoDB, and scoped IAM roles for functions.
Why choose this
Great for variable read traffic and rapid scaling with low operational overhead.
Container proposal (Fargate)
Components: ALB or API Gateway, ECS Fargate service running containerized API, Aurora or Aurora Serverless for relational needs, ECR for images, and CodePipeline for deployments.
Why choose this
Better for existing applications, long-running processes, or when you need control over runtime and dependencies.
Trade-off discussion: use serverless for lower ops and spiky traffic, containers for predictable loads or when the app requires runtime control. Validate the decision by measuring expected traffic, latency requirements for catalog reads, and how easily the codebase can be refactored into stateless functions.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Serverless and Containers
screens.narratorSegment: Keep three core concepts in mind. First, serverless offers operational simplicity and pay-per-use billing, making it ideal for short, event-driven tasks; design functions to be stateless and mitigate cold-starts when latency matters. Second, containers provide portability and control: package runtime and dependencies for consistent execution, and use ECS, Fargate, or EKS based on operational needs. Third, CI/CD and observability are non-negotiable: automate builds, tests, and deployments, scan images, and instrument code with metrics and tracing so you can measure cost and performance. These ideas guide practical decision-making during modernization, helping you map workloads to an architecture that balances speed of delivery, operational effort, and cost. As you finish this module, refer back to these concepts when drafting your architecture proposal and when designing pipelines and monitoring to validate your assumptions.

fullNarratorScript:
Modernization is about transforming how applications are designed and run so they take full advantage of the cloud. In this lesson we compare two dominant paradigms: serverless computing, where you hand operational concerns to the provider and pay for actual execution, and containerization, where you package runtime and dependencies for portability and control. You will learn core AWS services and when each approach fits common patterns like APIs, background processing, and long-running workloads. We’ll walk through a serverless A P I pattern that combines A P I Gateway, Lambda, and DynamoDB and a container workflow using Docker, Amazon ECS with Fargate, or Amazon EKS for Kubernetes. You’ll also see CI/CD integration using AWS Developer Tools and practical tuning tips for cost, performance, and observability. By the end you’ll be able to propose a modernization approach for a product catalog, explain trade-offs between pay-per-use and packaged portability, and identify key operational practices like rightsizing, tracing, and the principle of least privilege. Think about one legacy workload you know — which model would reduce operational overhead fastest and why?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to evaluate the benefits and trade-offs of serverless and container architectures, design event-driven APIs using Lambda and A P I Gateway, and implement containerized services on ECS, Fargate, or EKS. You will also integrate CI/CD pipelines that deploy serverless applications and container images, and apply cost and performance optimization techniques specific to each model. Each objective ties a capability to an observable outcome: design diagrams, deployment artifacts, and measurable optimizations. For example, you’ll practice creating a serverless A P I and a container image, then wire them into a pipeline that builds, tests, and deploys. You’ll learn when to prefer Lambda’s event-driven scaling over Fargate’s runtime control, and how provisioning choices affect latency and cost. These skills are practical; they let you reduce operational overhead or provide portability, depending on the business need. As you study, think about how you would validate each objective with a short test or hands-on task.

These applied objectives translate into artifacts and measurable outcomes. You will produce an event-driven A P I design that includes A P I Gateway routes, Lambda handlers, and a DynamoDB access pattern; a container image and deployment manifest for ECS Fargate or EKS; and a CI/CD pipeline that builds and deploys either a SAM package or a container image pushed to ECR. Measurement criteria include deployment time, cold-start latency for Lambda, per-invocation cost estimate, and container startup latency. We’ll show you how to instrument these outcomes with CloudWatch metrics and distributed tracing so you can verify improvements. A common misconception is that modernization always reduces cost — instead, modernization shifts costs and trade-offs: serverless can reduce idle infrastructure spend but may increase per-invocation costs for very high sustained throughput. Keep that in mind as you compare approaches and validate with simple metrics after deployment.

Serverless computing is a cloud execution model where the provider manages servers and capacity so developers can focus on code. AWS Lambda exemplifies this: you upload a function, configure triggers, and Lambda runs the code on demand while scaling automatically. Common serverless use cases include short-lived microservice endpoints, data transformation jobs triggered by storage events, mobile backends, and chatbots. A concrete example is an image thumbnailer: when an image is uploaded to object storage, an event triggers Lambda to resize and store thumbnails. That pattern removes the need to manage servers but brings specific constraints. Functions have maximum execution durations and require you to design for short-lived, stateless work. Cold starts occur when a function is invoked after a period of inactivity; provisioned concurrency can reduce cold-start latency for latency-sensitive endpoints. A common misconception is thinking Lambda is suitable for every workload: long-running processes, heavy G P U workloads, or apps needing custom kernel modules are better suited to containers or EC2. As you design serverless components, apply the principle of least privilege for IAM roles, decouple services with queues to handle bursts, and measure per-invocation cost against expected throughput. Which part of your application can be refactored into short, stateless functions first?

A common serverless pattern for APIs uses A P I Gateway to accept HTTP requests, Lambda for business logic, and DynamoDB for low-latency data storage. The request enters A P I Gateway which handles authentication, throttling, and caching, then forwards the event to a Lambda function. The function performs validation and reads or writes to DynamoDB. For asynchronous work, the function can publish events to SNS or EventBridge or push messages to SQS for buffered processing. This pattern provides clear integration points: A P I Gateway for ingress policy, Lambda for execution with scoped IAM permissions to access a specific DynamoDB table, and messaging services to decouple long-running or unreliable downstream tasks. A concrete scenario is a product catalog read: a GET request to /products/{id} triggers a Lambda that reads DynamoDB with a single-key query and returns results. Misconceptions include assuming synchronous invocation is always best; for durability and smoothing bursts, buffer writes with SQS or event buses. When designing this flow, consider cold-starts for user-facing routes, set appropriate retries, and apply caching where reads are common. How would you design retries and idempotency for write operations to prevent duplication?

Infrastructure-as-code lets you describe serverless resources and deploy them reproducibly. The Serverless Application Model, or SAM, provides a concise way to declare Lambda functions, A P I events, and DynamoDB tables. The template example in this chapter shows two functions, GetProductFunction and CreateProductFunction, each wired to an A P I event and granted the appropriate DynamoDB policy. When you deploy with a SAM workflow, the template becomes the single source of truth for configuration like memory, timeout, and attached policies. A concrete walkthrough: the GetProductFunction includes an Api event with a GET path mapping, which tells A P I Gateway to route GET requests for that path to this function. The ProductsTable resource uses PAY_PER_REQUEST billing to match serverless cost behavior. A common misunderstanding is forgetting to scope IAM policies — grant only the minimal permissions each function needs. After deployment, test the A P I and inspect CloudWatch logs to verify handler logic and identify cold-start patterns. In practice, keep templates modular and parameterized to support multiple environments. SAM Template Example for a Serverless API means sam templates define functions, events, and resources as code so deployments are repeatable and auditable.. In practical terms, understanding resources, events, and permissions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Containerization packages an application and all its dependencies into a lightweight, portable unit that runs consistently across environments. Docker is the de facto tool for building container images. Containers solve the "it works on my machine" problem by including runtime, libraries, and configuration in a single image. A short Dockerfile for a Node. js app illustrates the pattern: start from a base image, set a working directory, copy package metadata, install dependencies, copy source, expose a port, and define the startup command. This produces an image you can run locally and then push to a registry such as ECR. An important distinction is that containers provide greater control over runtime and long-running processes compared with serverless functions. They are preferable when you need custom runtime dependencies, long execution times, or G P U support. A misconception is equating containers with zero ops; orchestration and node management remain concerns unless you use a managed mode like Fargate. When creating images, optimize the build for smaller image sizes and security scanning so deployments remain fast and safe. What dependency could you remove or slim to reduce your image size?

AWS provides multiple container orchestration options: Amazon ECS for a native, simple orchestration experience; AWS Fargate to run containers without managing instances; and Amazon EKS for Kubernetes-managed workloads. ECS is straightforward and integrates well with other AWS primitives. Choose ECS when you want simple task definition and cluster management with AWS integration. Fargate removes instance management completely — it is useful when you want the container model but prefer serverless operations for container workloads. EKS is the managed Kubernetes control plane: use EKS when you require Kubernetes APIs, portability across clouds, or advanced scheduling and extensibility. An example decision: if your team relies on Kubernetes tooling and helm charts, EKS preserves that workflow; if your application needs serverless-style operations and you do not need Kubernetes features, choose Fargate. A common misconception is that Fargate and Lambda are interchangeable; they are not. Fargate runs containers and supports longer running processes and custom runtimes, while Lambda is designed for short-lived functions. Consider operational skill, portability needs, runtime requirements, and cost model when deciding which orchestration fits your modernization plan. ECS, Fargate, and EKS — Choosing an orchestration model means pick ecs for native simplicity, fargate for serverless containers, and eks when kubernetes features and portability are required.. In practical terms, managed orchestration options and when to pick each. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Creating a containerized application follows a short cycle: author a Dockerfile, build an image, push it to a registry like ECR, and deploy via a task definition or Kubernetes manifest. The example Dockerfile in this chapter uses a Node. js base image, installs dependencies, and exposes a port. After building locally with the docker build command, tag the image for ECR and push it. In ECS, create a task definition that references the ECR image and then run the task as a service either on EC2-backed clusters or on Fargate for serverless operations. For Kubernetes, you apply a deployment manifest and expose it with a LoadBalancer service. A typical command sequence is: build, tag with the ECR repository URI, docker push, then update the service to use the new image. Common mistakes include not scanning images for vulnerabilities and embedding credentials in the image. Always use IAM roles for tasks and scan images before pushing. Consider using multi-stage builds to reduce image size and speed up pulls, which improves startup time in production. Building and Deploying a Container Image means build images with optimized dockerfiles, push to ecr, and deploy via ecs/fargate or eks with proper task roles and image scanning.. In practical terms, dockerfile, build, push to ecr, and run on ecs/fargate. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

CI/CD pipelines automate the repetitive steps of building, testing, and deploying modern applications. AWS Developer Tools—CodeCommit, CodeBuild, CodeDeploy, and CodePipeline—integrate directly with serverless and container targets. For serverless apps, a typical pipeline builds code, packages a SAM artifact, runs unit and integration tests, and then executes a deployment step that updates the CloudFormation stack or SAM application. For containers, the pipeline builds a Docker image in CodeBuild, pushes it to ECR, and then updates an ECS task definition or triggers a Kubernetes rollout. Key CI/CD practices include immutable artifacts, automated tests, and deployment strategies such as blue/green or canary to reduce risk. A common misconception is that CI/CD only speeds delivery; it also enforces consistency and improves rollback safety. Ensure pipelines run image scans and integration tests before promoting artifacts to production. When integrating serverless deployments, consider how to manage permissions so the pipeline has least privilege and can perform only its required tasks. What tests would you add to validate a serverless function's behavior in a pipeline? CI/CD for Serverless and Containers means automate building, testing, and deploying serverless or container artifacts with gated stages, artifact immutability, and safe deployment strategies.. In practical terms, automating builds, tests, and deployments with aws developer tools. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. Keep three core concepts in mind. First, serverless offers operational simplicity and pay-per-use billing, making it ideal for short, event-driven tasks; design functions to be stateless and mitigate cold-starts when latency matters. Second, containers provide portability and control: package runtime and dependencies for consistent execution, and use ECS, Fargate, or EKS based on operational needs. Third, CI/CD and observability are non-negotiable: automate builds, tests, and deployments, scan images, and instrument code with metrics and tracing so you can measure cost and performance.
